title: Domino's Pepperoni Pizza
description: The classic crowd-pleaser: a generous layer of pepperoni over 100% real mozzarella and signature tomato sauce, on your choice of crust.
fullContent:
The Pizza Everyone Orders First

Pepperoni is the most-ordered item at Domino's, and it earns that. Signature tomato sauce, 100% real mozzarella, and pepperoni that curls and crisps at the edges in the oven. Nothing clever, and that's the point — it's the pizza nobody at the table objects to.

What most people never do is look at what's actually in it, or notice that the same pizza can cost several dollars more or less depending only on how they ordered it. Both are worth thirty seconds.

The Numbers

SizeSlicesExample priceCal / slice
Small 10"6~$8.99~230
Medium 12"8~$10.99~240
Large 14"8~$12.99~280

A large Hand Tossed pepperoni slice sits around 280 calories, with published sources ranging from about 275 to 300 — treat it as roughly 280 rather than an exact figure. A whole large is near 2,240.

The trap in that table is the slice size. Two large slices is not the same as two small slices; it's closer to three. "Just one slice" means different things at different sizes, which is why people underestimate a large pizza so consistently.

The Sodium Figure Nobody Checks

Roughly 600mg of sodium in a large slice — about a quarter of the 2,300mg daily limit US dietary guidelines suggest for an adult.

Four slices is a full day's sodium. For most people that's a more meaningful number than the calorie count, because four slices of a large pizza is an entirely normal dinner rather than an excessive one.

It's also worth knowing that Ultimate Pepperoni is substantially saltier — published figures put it near 830mg a slice against roughly 600mg for standard pepperoni, because it carries two layers of pepperoni plus extra cheeses. If you're choosing between them and sodium matters, that's a 40% jump.

On the other side of the ledger: about 12g of protein and 35g of carbohydrate per slice. A couple of slices is a genuine meal rather than empty calories, which is worth saying on a menu where plenty of items aren't.

The Crust Changes Everything

This is where people order on autopilot and leave the easiest saving on the table. Pepperoni tastes genuinely different depending on what's underneath it — and the calorie difference is large.

CrustWhat you getRoughly
Hand TossedSoft, pillowy, the default~280 / slice
Crunchy ThinLight, crisp, less bread~60–90 fewer / slice
Handmade PanThick, buttery, richestHeavier
Brooklyn StyleBig, foldable slicesL and XL only
Gluten FreeSmall only, shared kitchen—

Switching to Crunchy Thin costs nothing and removes roughly 500 calories from a large pizza. Same price, same toppings, same pizza otherwise. It's the single best-value change on the Domino's menu, and it's free.

Add light cheese — also free — and you take another 25 or so off each slice. Together those two changes bring a large pepperoni down by around 700 calories without touching what you actually ordered. Our crust guide covers how each one tastes.

Never Pay Menu Price

Pepperoni is the item most consistently included in Domino's offers, which means the menu price is close to the worst price you can pay for it.

A large pepperoni inside a Mix & Match style deal, or through a carryout special, routinely lands several dollars below the menu figure — for an identical pizza from the same oven. The only thing separating those two prices is which screen you ordered from.

Two rules that cover most situations:

  • Ordering one pizza: check the carryout special first
  • Ordering anything else alongside it: build the whole order inside a multi-item offer rather than adding items afterwards

Our deal comparison works through which offer fits which basket, including the trap where adding a third item to unlock a lower per-item price leaves you paying more overall.

Making It Your Own

A plain pepperoni is a blank canvas, and the useful customisations are cheaper than people assume:

  • Free: crust change, sauce swap, light or normal cheese, half-and-half toppings
  • Paid: extra toppings (~$1.50–$3.00 each), extra cheese
  • Best value addition: a vegetable rather than a second meat — same price, a fraction of the calories

The sauce swap is the most underused of these. Ordering pepperoni on a garlic Parmesan or BBQ base costs nothing and produces a genuinely different pizza — see our toppings and sauces guide.

If you find yourself adding three or four toppings, stop and compare with a specialty pizza instead. Per-topping charges compound quickly, and the ExtravaganZZa exists precisely because eight toppings priced individually is expensive.

Who It Suits

  • Feeding a mixed group — the pizza nobody refuses
  • Anyone who wants a reliable order rather than an interesting one
  • Deal ordering — it qualifies for more offers than anything else on the menu
  • A base to customise, rather than an end point

And who it doesn't:

  • Vegetarians, or anyone avoiding pork — pepperoni is a pork product
  • Anyone watching sodium closely — four slices is a day's worth
  • Anyone bored of it — a sauce swap or a specialty pizza fixes that for little or no money

Rounding Out the Order

A pepperoni pizza rarely travels alone. The sensible additions depend on what you want it to do:

  • Cheapest addition: Parmesan Bread Bites, around $4.99 for sixteen pieces
  • Most indulgent: Stuffed Cheesy Bread — but treat it as replacing two slices, not joining them
  • Cheapest drink: a 2-litre rather than bottles, at roughly a third the cost per ounce

Prices and nutrition figures here are examples and approximations drawn from published data, and sources vary. Domino's stores are independently franchised and set their own prices — confirm at checkout. Full calorie comparisons across the menu are in our calories guide.

title: Domino's ExtravaganZZa Pizza
description: Domino's most loaded specialty pizza: pepperoni, ham, Italian sausage, beef, onions, green peppers, mushrooms and black olives with extra cheese.
fullContent:
The Most Loaded Pizza on the Menu

Four meats and four vegetables: pepperoni, ham, Italian sausage, beef, onions, green peppers, mushrooms and black olives, with extra cheese. The ExtravaganZZa is the maximalist option, and it's the most food per slice Domino's sells.

It eats like a meal rather than a snack — three slices is a proper dinner, not a portion of one. That's the appeal, and it's also where the numbers get interesting.

The Numbers

ExtravaganZZaStandard pepperoni
Calories / large slice~380~280
Sodium / large slice~900mg~600mg
Protein / slice~16g~12g
Example price (large)~$16.99~$12.99

At roughly 380 calories a slice this is the heaviest pizza Domino's makes, about 100 above standard pepperoni. A whole large lands near 3,040.

The Sodium Story

The calorie figure is the one people look at. The sodium figure is the one that matters.

Around 900mg per large slice — that's 39% of the 2,300mg daily limit US dietary guidelines suggest for an adult, in a single slice.

Three slices is more than a full day's sodium. And three slices of a loaded pizza is not a large meal; it's a normal one. That's the genuinely useful thing to know about this pizza, and it appears nowhere a customer would see it.

None of which means don't order it. It means that if you eat this occasionally it's unremarkable, and if you're managing blood pressure or watching sodium on medical advice, this specific pizza is the one to be aware of. Two slices with a salad is a different proposition from four slices on their own.

Don't Build It Yourself

A common and expensive mistake, because people assume build-your-own is always cheaper.

Route to the same pizzaExample cost
Large base + 8 toppings at ~$2.50 each~$31.99
ExtravaganZZa from the specialty menu~$16.99

About fifteen dollars more to assemble the identical pizza yourself. Per-topping charges compound fast, and the specialty menu exists precisely because Domino's prices these combinations as a bundle rather than as eight separate additions.

The corollary is more useful still: removals are normally free. An ExtravaganZZa without the olives costs the same as one with them. So starting from this pizza and stripping out what your table won't eat is almost always cheaper than building up from a plain cheese base — and you keep the specialty price.

Order It on Thin Crust

The recommendation that changes this pizza most, and it costs nothing.

With eight toppings and extra cheese, a thick base makes the whole thing heavy and awkward to eat — the crust competes with the toppings rather than carrying them. Crunchy Thin balances it, letting the toppings do the work, and it removes roughly 60 to 90 calories a slice on the menu's heaviest pizza.

Same price, better pizza, meaningfully lighter. Our crust guide covers the full range.

ExtravaganZZa or MeatZZa?

The two get confused constantly, and the difference is simple.

  • MeatZZa — the same four meats, no vegetables, around 350 calories a slice
  • ExtravaganZZa — those meats plus onions, peppers, mushrooms and olives, around 380

If someone at your table picks vegetables off their pizza, order the MeatZZa. If you want the fuller version, this is it. They're normally priced the same, so it's purely about whether the vegetables are wanted.

The full specialty lineup, with what's on each one, is in our specialty pizzas guide.

Never at Menu Price

A large specialty at around $16.99 is the most expensive way to buy this pizza. Specialty pizzas frequently appear in offers at close to $9.99 for a medium, and a percentage-off promotion applied to the higher menu price tends to produce the biggest discount of all.

Worth knowing: multi-item deals are priced around a two-topping build, so specialty recipes are sometimes excluded or carry an upcharge. That's exactly when a percentage-off offer becomes the better route. Our deal comparison works through which offer suits which order.

Who It Suits

  • Big appetites — the most food per slice on the menu
  • A table that wants one pizza to cover everything — meat and vegetables in the same order
  • Anyone bored of pepperoni who doesn't want to pay per topping to fix it
  • Sharing, where two or three slices each is the plan

And who it doesn't:

  • Anyone watching sodium — three slices exceeds a day's limit
  • Fussy eaters, unless you strip toppings out, which is free
  • Vegetarians — four meats; Pacific Veggie is the meat-free specialty
  • Anyone who wanted a light meal — this is the heaviest pizza here

Where It Sits

Against the rest of the pizza menu, this is the top of the range in both senses — the most toppings and the heaviest numbers. Against a plain pepperoni, it's about four dollars more at menu price and 100 calories a slice heavier, in exchange for a great deal more food.

The honest summary: it's a genuinely good pizza and a poor default. Order it when you want a loaded pizza and you're sharing it; order pepperoni when you just want dinner.

title: Domino's Philly Cheese Steak Pizza
description: Tender steak, fresh onions, green peppers and mushrooms over a creamy blend of American and provolone cheese instead of tomato sauce.
fullContent:
A Cheesesteak That Thinks It's a Pizza

Now here's something a little different. The Philly Cheese Steak Pizza throws out the rulebook and skips tomato sauce entirely. Instead, it's built on a creamy blend of American and provolone cheese, then loaded with tender steak, fresh onions, green peppers and mushrooms. The result? It tastes far more like an actual Philly cheesesteak sandwich than a traditional pizza. If you've ever found yourself a bit bored of red-sauce pizzas, this one's going to feel like a revelation.

What I really like about it is that it doesn't pretend to be something it's not. It leans all the way into the cheesesteak idea, and it commits. That confidence is exactly why it's built a loyal following among people who want their pizza to surprise them a little.

Why It Stands Out

Two things make this pizza genuinely different from almost everything else on the menu, and they matter more than you'd think.

What's DifferentWhy It Matters
No tomato saucePerfect if you're not a red-sauce fan
American + provolone baseRich, creamy, true cheesesteak flavor
Steak, no porkA solid pick for pork-free households

That last point deserves a mention. Because it's built on steak with no pork, the Philly Cheese Steak is a genuinely good option for households that skip pork — and it doesn't feel like a compromise while doing it.

The Best Way to Order It

Because the topping load is rich and cheesy, a lot of fans swear by the Crunchy Thin Crust here. It keeps the base crisp underneath all that provolone instead of going soft, and the contrast is lovely. Hand Tossed works fine too if you like it pillowy, but thin crust is the move I'd steer you toward for this particular pie. As for price, it's a specialty pizza, so it sits a bit higher on the menu — but it usually qualifies for Mix & Match, which drags it down to the same per-item rate as a basic pizza. Check the current deals before you order and you'll rarely pay full price.

Nutrition and Allergens, Honestly

Expect roughly 300 to 330 calories per Large slice, which is fairly reasonable for how rich it tastes. It contains wheat and milk — the milk comes from that double dose of cheese — and includes beef. As I mentioned, there's no pork, which some diners specifically look for. If you want to trim it down, the usual two tricks apply: ask for light cheese, or order it on thin crust. Both help without gutting the flavor.

What to Pair It With

The Philly Cheese Steak is savory and satisfying, so it plays well with something a little different alongside it. I'd pair it with Boneless Chicken and a drink through a deal, or add Stuffed Cheesy Bread for a proper two-item meal that fills the table. Since it's a bit of an adventurous pick, it also pairs nicely next to a plain pepperoni when you're feeding a mixed crowd.

The Bottom Line

The Philly Cheese Steak Pizza is for anyone craving something savory, cheesy, and refreshingly off the beaten path. No red sauce, no pork, all flavor. Order it thin-crust through a deal and you've got a genuinely different dinner without paying extra for the privilege. As always, these are example prices — this is an independent, unofficial guide, so let the official Domino's app confirm the real total at checkout.

title: Domino's Stuffed Cheesy Bread
description: Oven-baked bread stuffed with a blend of cheeses and seasoned with garlic and parsley, served with a dipping sauce.
fullContent:
The Side That Steals the Show

Let's give the sides their due, because Stuffed Cheesy Bread might be the best thing at Domino's that isn't technically a pizza. Here's the magic: it's soft, oven-baked bread with a blend of cheeses baked right inside, then brushed with garlic-and-parsley seasoning and cut into shareable strips. That inside part is the whole point. Plain bread twists put cheese on top; this stuffs it in, so every single piece pulls apart in that gooey, stringy way that makes everyone at the table reach for one more. It comes with marinara for dipping by default, and you can swap for garlic or ranch.

I'll be honest — I've ordered pizza plenty of times mostly as an excuse to also get the Stuffed Cheesy Bread. It's that good. If you're a first-timer at Domino's and you only try one side, make it this one.

The Varieties Worth Knowing

The original is the classic, but Domino's gives you a few ways to dress it up, and each one changes the vibe.

VarietyWhat's AddedGood For
OriginalJust the cheese blendPurists and picky eaters
Bacon & JalapeñoSmoky bacon, a little heatSpice fans (contains pork)
Spinach & FetaSpinach, tangy fetaA slightly grown-up twist

How Much You Get, and What It Costs

A single order comes cut into 8 pieces, which works as a shared appetizer for two to four people or a generous snack for one hungry person who isn't sharing (no judgment). On price, here's the good news: Stuffed Cheesy Bread frequently qualifies for the $6.99 Each and Mix & Match deals, which is comfortably the cheapest way to add it to an order. Tacking it onto a pizza through a deal is one of those little moves that makes the whole meal feel bigger without the total jumping much. Peek at the current deals before you order.

Nutrition and Allergens

Each piece runs roughly 140 to 180 calories depending on the variety, so it's a treat rather than a health food — but you knew that. It contains wheat and milk, and the bacon-jalapeño version adds pork. Good to know on the dips, too: the marinara is vegetarian-friendly, while ranch and garlic dips contain milk and egg. If you're sharing across a few people, one order stretches further than you'd expect, which helps on both calories and cost.

What to Pair It With

Stuffed Cheesy Bread is the classic wingman to a good pizza. It's the natural companion to a Pepperoni or the loaded ExtravaganZZa. For a full family spread, add a 2-liter of Coke and run the whole order through Mix & Match so the side basically pays for itself in savings. It also gives the non-pizza eater at the table something to reach for, which every family knows is worth its weight in gold.

The Bottom Line

Stuffed Cheesy Bread is proof that the best part of a Domino's order isn't always the pizza. Gooey, shareable, and cheap when you grab it inside a deal — it's an easy yes on almost any order. Prices here are examples, so let the official Domino's app confirm the real number at checkout. This is an independent, unofficial guide, but the recommendation is heartfelt: get the cheesy bread.

title: Domino's Boneless Chicken
description: Lightly breaded, oven-baked all-white-meat boneless chicken, served plain or tossed in a signature sauce.
fullContent:
The Most Versatile Thing on the Menu

Here's a little secret: Boneless Chicken might be the most flexible order at Domino's. It's lightly breaded, oven-baked, all-white-meat chicken that you can grab plain with a dip or tossed in a sauce. Want an appetizer? Done. A lighter main instead of pizza? Also done. A protein boost alongside a pie through a deal? That too. Not many items pull triple duty like this, and that's exactly why it's a smart thing to keep in your back pocket.

And to clear up a common mix-up — yes, boneless chicken is genuinely boneless. It's white-meat chicken with no bones, which makes it completely different from Domino's bone-in wings. No gnawing, no mess, just easy pieces you can dunk and go.

Pick Your Sauce

This is where boneless chicken gets fun, because the sauce completely changes the personality of the order.

SauceThe Vibe
Plain (with a dip)Simple, kid-friendly, you control the flavor
Hot BuffaloClassic tangy heat
Sweet BBQSweet, smoky, crowd-pleasing
Garlic ParmesanSavory and rich
Mango HabaneroSweet up front, spicy on the finish

My move for a mixed group? Order it plain and let everyone dip it their own way. For myself, it's Sweet BBQ every time, no debate.

Portions and Smart Pricing

Domino's serves Boneless Chicken in an 8-piece order and larger shareable counts. An 8-piece works nicely as a solo meal or a side for two. Here's the value angle that makes it a favorite of mine: it's one of the best Mix & Match and $6.99 Each picks going, because it rounds out a pizza order with real protein for a low add-on cost. When a pizza alone won't quite satisfy the table, a deal-priced order of boneless chicken fixes it cheaply. Check the current deals and stay in Rewards while you're at it.

Nutrition and Allergens

Plain Boneless Chicken runs roughly 60 to 70 calories per piece before any sauce, which makes it one of the lighter ways to add protein to a Domino's order — order it plain and it's genuinely reasonable. The sauces add calories and sodium, and the Sweet BBQ and Mango Habanero are the sugariest of the bunch, so keep that in mind if you're watching intake. On allergens, it contains wheat, milk, soy and egg from the breading, so it isn't gluten-free despite being 'just chicken.'

What to Pair It With

Boneless chicken slots into almost any order. Pair it with a Pepperoni Pizza and a drink for the classic combo, or use it as the protein in a lighter meal alongside a thin-crust veggie pizza. Add Stuffed Cheesy Bread and you've built a proper shareable spread. For the full lineup of chicken and everything else, the menu and prices page has it all.

The Bottom Line

Boneless Chicken is the quiet workhorse of the Domino's menu — flexible, deal-friendly, and lighter than most sides when you keep it plain. It's the easiest way to turn 'just a pizza' into a real meal without spending much. As always, prices are examples, so let the official Domino's app confirm the real total. This is an independent, unofficial guide, here to help you order well.

title: Domino's Drinks Menu & Prices
description: Coca-Cola bottles and 2-liters at Domino's — prices, calories, which size is actually better value, and how drinks work inside a deal.
fullContent:
The Only Drink Decision That Matters

Drinks are the part of the order people add without thinking, and it is the one place where thirty seconds of attention reliably saves money. Domino's stocks Coca-Cola beverages in two formats — individual 20 oz bottles and 2-liter bottles — and the gap between them per ounce is larger than almost any other choice on the menu.

Prices here are examples. Drinks are franchise-priced and vary more between stores than pizzas do, so confirm at checkout.

The Per-Ounce Maths

This is the whole point of the page, so here it is plainly.

OptionVolumeExample priceCost per ounce
20 oz bottle20 oz~$2.49~12.5¢
2-liter bottle67.6 oz~$3.49~5.2¢

The 2-liter is roughly two and a half times better value per ounce. Another way to see it: a 2-liter holds nearly three and a half 20 oz bottles. Buying three individual bottles costs around $7.47; one 2-liter with more liquid in it costs about $3.49.

So the rule is simple. Ordering for one person who wants one drink: a bottle is fine. Ordering for two or more people: the 2-liter, every time. There is no situation where three separate bottles beats a 2-liter on price.

What's Actually Available

DrinkNotes
Coca-ColaThe default; full sugar
Diet CokeZero calorie, classic diet flavour
Coke Zero SugarZero calorie, closer to regular Coke
SpriteLemon-lime, the usual non-cola pick
Fanta OrangeSweetest of the lineup; popular with children
Barq's Root BeerDivisive, and the one most often out of stock
Bottled waterAround $2 at most stores

The lineup is Coca-Cola across the board, which is worth knowing if you specifically want Pepsi products — that is Pizza Hut's supplier, not Domino's. Availability of individual flavours is set per store, so the list in your app is the accurate one.

The Cheapest Calorie Saving on the Menu

Most people optimise the pizza and ignore the drink, which is backwards.

DrinkCaloriesRoughly equal to
20 oz regular soda~240–250A slice of large cheese pizza
2-liter regular, per 8 oz glass~100A dipping cup of ranch
Diet Coke / Coke Zero0—
Bottled water0—

A 20 oz regular soda carries about as many calories as an extra slice of pizza. Switching to a zero-sugar option removes roughly 240 calories from the order and changes nothing about the food. Nothing else on the Domino's menu gives you a saving that large for that little sacrifice — see our calories and nutrition guide for how that compares against the pizza itself.

Worth flagging for group orders: a 2-liter of regular soda is around 800 calories in the bottle. Split four ways that is a modest 200 each, but a 2-liter shared between two people is a different number entirely.

Drinks Inside a Deal

This is where people quietly overpay. Drinks are frequently a qualifying item in Mix & Match style offers, which means two things:

  • Adding a drink inside the deal often costs less than adding it at menu price at the end
  • A drink can be the cheapest way to reach the item count an offer requires — if a deal needs three items and you want two pizzas, a 2-liter is usually the cheapest third

The mistake is building the order, hitting checkout, then adding a drink on top at full price. Build it into the deal instead. Our Mix & Match explainer covers how the item counting works, and the coupons page has what is currently running.

How Much to Order

  • One person: a 20 oz bottle, or a 2-liter if you want leftovers
  • Two people: one 2-liter — cheaper than two bottles and there is more of it
  • Three to four: one 2-liter covers it at roughly 12–16 oz each
  • Five or more: two 2-liters, still cheaper than individual bottles
  • Mixed preferences: one regular 2-liter plus one zero-sugar beats buying four different bottles

That last one is the practical tip for families. Two 2-liters in different varieties costs around $7 and satisfies almost any table; four individual bottles costs around $10 and satisfies four people exactly once.

A Few Practical Notes

  • Bottles arrive at room temperature more often than people expect. Stores are not refrigerating everything, and a 2-liter that has been sitting in a warm store is not cold when it reaches you. If it matters, plan for ice
  • Carryout gives you the option to skip drinks entirely. A supermarket 2-liter costs a fraction of the delivered price — if you are already going out, buying the drink elsewhere is the cheapest route of all
  • Drinks are the most price-variable item on the menu. Two stores in the same city can differ by a dollar on the same 2-liter
  • Zero-sugar options are the same price as their full-sugar equivalents, so the calorie saving costs nothing

The Short Version

title: Domino's Chicken Alfredo Pasta
description: Penne baked with grilled chicken breast in a creamy Alfredo sauce — the mildest of Domino's four pastas and the second lightest.
fullContent:
The Mild One

Chicken Alfredo is Domino's most popular pasta and the one most people default to: penne tossed with grilled chicken breast in a creamy Alfredo sauce, then baked in the same conveyor oven as the pizzas rather than boiled and plated. That oven finish is why the top arrives slightly browned and bubbling instead of looking like pasta reheated in a pan.

Among the four pastas it occupies the safe middle: milder than the sausage marinara, richer than the vegetable one, and the least likely to surprise anyone at the table.

Price and Calories

Served inExample priceCalories
Dish~$7.99~620
Bread bowl~$8.99~690

A correction worth making, because this page previously said otherwise. The bread bowl adds far less than people assume — published figures show roughly 620 in a dish against 690 in a bowl, a step of about 70 calories rather than the several hundred a hollowed-out loaf implies.

The likely explanation is that the pasta portion inside a bowl is smaller, offsetting the bread. Sources disagree more on bread bowl entries than on dish entries, so if the exact number matters to you, build it in the app and read the live figure.

Which means the bread bowl question is genuinely about appetite and novelty rather than calories. It's about a dollar more for an edible bowl. If you're hungry, it's a reasonable dollar; if you're not, the dish is the same pasta.

Where It Sits Among the Four Pastas

Pasta (dish)CaloriesSauce
Pasta Primavera~530–550Cream, vegetables
Chicken Alfredo~620Cream, chicken
Italian Sausage Marinara~690Tomato, pork sausage
Chicken Carbonara~690Cream, richest

Two things are worth pulling out of that. Chicken Alfredo is lighter than the tomato-based pasta, which reverses what most people assume — cream sounds heavier than tomato, but the sausage is doing more work than the sauce is. And three of the four pastas are cream-based, which is a genuine gap: there's exactly one tomato pasta on the menu and it contains pork.

The Leftovers Problem

The main practical drawback, and nobody puts it on a menu.

Cream sauces split when reheated. The fat separates from the liquid, the texture turns grainy, and a microwave is particularly unkind. If you're ordering for one person and expect to eat half tomorrow, this is the wrong pasta.

  • Best fix: an oven at low heat, covered, which holds the emulsion together
  • Worst approach: a microwave on full power
  • Better plan: order the marinara pasta instead, which reheats without any of this

This is the single most useful reason to choose between Alfredo and marinara, and it has nothing to do with which tastes better.

How It Tastes

Rich, mild and cheese-forward. The Alfredo is a thick cream sauce rather than a thin one, so it clings to the penne and the chicken instead of pooling at the bottom of the dish. There is no chilli heat at all, which is exactly why it works for children and for anyone who finds the sausage marinara too sharp.

The chicken is grilled breast meat, diced rather than shredded. It's the lean element in an otherwise rich dish, and it's the reason this reads as a meal rather than a side — there's enough protein in it to be dinner.

Who It Suits

  • Someone who doesn't want pizza but is ordering with a group that does
  • Children — mild, familiar, no heat
  • Lunch — the dish version travels well and needs no sharing
  • Anyone who finds tomato sauces too acidic

And who it doesn't:

  • Anyone planning on leftovers — the sauce won't survive the reheat
  • Vegetarians — the chicken is central; Pasta Primavera is the meat-free option
  • Anyone avoiding dairy — the sauce is cream-based and there's no substitute
  • Anyone counting calories tightly — at ~620 it's a full meal, comparable to two slices of large cheese pizza

Ordering It Well

  • Build it into a deal rather than adding it after. Pasta is normally Mix & Match eligible, so it costs less inside an offer than bolted on at menu price — our deal comparison covers which offer fits which basket
  • Choose dish or bowl on appetite, now that we know the calorie difference is small
  • Eat it fresh. More than most items here, this one is best on the day
  • Skip a bread side alongside it. Pasta plus bread is a lot of the same thing in one meal — and if you take the bread bowl, you've already had it
  • Check your store carries it. Pasta availability varies between franchises more than pizza does

Build Your Own Instead?

Worth knowing that Domino's also offers a build-your-own penne, where you pick the sauce and add toppings. If you want the Alfredo base with different additions — spinach, mushrooms, bacon — that's the route, and it costs about the same.

It's also the only way to get a cream-free, meat-free pasta here: Robust Inspired Tomato Sauce with vegetable toppings and no cheese is the vegan option, which our vegetarian and vegan guide covers in full.

Where It Sits on the Menu

Against the other pastas, this is the safe, mild, middle choice — and the one to avoid if leftovers are likely. Against the wider menu, roughly 620 calories for about $7.99 is a complete meal for one person at a fair price, lighter than a small pizza at close to 1,200 and comparable to an oven-baked sandwich.

title: Domino's Italian Sausage Marinara Pasta
description: Penne baked with Italian sausage in a tomato marinara sauce — Domino's tomato-based pasta, and the alternative to the cream-sauce dishes.
fullContent:
The Tomato One

Domino's pasta menu splits neatly down the middle: two cream-sauce dishes, one tomato, and one vegetable. Italian Sausage Marinara is the tomato one — penne baked with crumbled Italian sausage in a marinara-style sauce and finished with cheese.

It's baked in the same conveyor oven as the pizzas rather than boiled and plated, which is why the top comes out slightly browned and bubbling instead of looking like pasta from a pan.

What It Costs and What's In It

Served inExample priceCalories
Dish~$7.99~690–700
Bread bowl~$8.99~730 (sources vary)

A note on that calorie figure, because it's worth being straight about. Independent nutrition databases put the dish between roughly 680 and 730, and Domino's own published guide has listed 700. So call it about 700 and don't treat any single number as exact. The bread bowl entries disagree more between sources than the dish does — if you're tracking intake closely, build the order in the app and read the live figure.

Sausage, Not Spice

The most common wrong expectation about this dish. "Italian sausage" describes a seasoning profile, not heat. What you get is fennel, garlic and black pepper — savoury and aromatic rather than hot. Nobody who ordered this hoping for a spicy pasta has been happy about it.

The sausage is crumbled rather than sliced, which matters more than it sounds: it distributes through the penne instead of sitting in lumps, so you get sausage flavour in most forkfuls rather than in a few.

Marinara or Alfredo?

This is the actual decision most people are making at the pasta screen, so here it is properly.

Italian Sausage MarinaraChicken Alfredo
SauceTomatoCream
ProteinPork sausageGrilled chicken
Calories (dish)~690–700~620
FlavourSavoury, seasonedRich, mild
ReheatsWellPoorly — sauce splits

Two things worth pulling out. The Alfredo is actually the lighter dish, which surprises people who assume tomato always beats cream — the sausage is doing the work here, not the sauce. And marinara is the clear winner on leftovers, which brings us to the genuinely useful part of this page.

The Reheating Advantage

If you are likely to have leftovers, order this one.

Cream sauces split when reheated. Alfredo and Carbonara go grainy and oily in a microwave — the fat separates from the liquid and there's no getting it back. Tomato sauces don't have that problem, because there's no emulsion to break.

  • Microwave: fine for this dish, poor for the cream ones
  • Oven at low heat: better still — cover it so the top doesn't dry out
  • Next day: genuinely good, which is not true of the Alfredo

Nobody puts this on a menu, but for anyone ordering for one person and expecting to eat half of it tomorrow, it's the single most practical reason to pick this pasta over the others.

Who It Suits

  • Anyone who finds cream sauces heavy — this is the alternative on the menu
  • Someone in a group who doesn't want pizza — it's a proper meal rather than a side
  • Leftovers — the only pasta here that's still good reheated
  • Lunch — the dish version travels well and needs no sharing

And who it doesn't:

  • Vegetarians. The sausage is pork and it's the point of the dish, not a topping — Pasta Primavera is the meat-free pasta
  • Anyone avoiding pork, for the same reason
  • Anyone avoiding dairy or wheat. Cheese and penne are both structural here, and everything is made in a shared kitchen
  • Anyone expecting heat. It isn't a spicy dish

Ordering It Well

  • Put it inside a deal, not beside one. Pasta is usually a qualifying item in Mix & Match style offers, so adding it within the deal costs less than bolting it on at menu price at the end. Our deal comparison covers which offer fits which basket
  • Decide dish or bread bowl on appetite, not price. The dollar difference is small; the difference in how full you'll be is not
  • Check it's on your store's menu. Pasta availability varies more between franchises than pizza does
  • If it's for one person as a whole meal, it works on its own. Adding a bread side to a pasta dish is a lot of carbohydrate for one sitting

Against the Rest of the Menu

Worth a moment of perspective on where this sits. At roughly 700 calories for about $7.99, it's a full meal for one person at a fair price — comparable to an oven-baked sandwich and lighter than a small pizza, which runs closer to 1,200.

Against the other pastas: Pasta Primavera is the lightest and the only vegetarian one, Chicken Alfredo is the mild cream option, and Chicken Carbonara is the richest. Prices are generally level across all four, so this is a flavour decision rather than a value one. The full lineup with prices is in our sides menu guide.

title: Domino's Pasta Primavera
description: Penne baked with spinach, mushrooms, onions and tomatoes in a creamy sauce — Domino's meat-free pasta, and the lightest of the four.
fullContent:
The Meat-Free One

Domino's pasta menu has four dishes and only one without meat in it. Pasta Primavera is that one — penne baked with baby spinach, mushrooms, onions and diced tomatoes in a creamy sauce, finished with cheese.

If you're the vegetarian in a group ordering pizza, this is your hot alternative to picking at a bread side. That's genuinely its main job, and it does it well.

The Name Is Misleading

Worth clearing up first, because it's the most common wrong assumption about this dish.

"Primavera" plus a list of vegetables suggests something light and tomato-based. It isn't. It's a cream-sauce pasta with vegetables in it. The vegetables are real and there are plenty of them, but the sauce doing the work is creamy, not marinara.

So if what you actually want is a tomato pasta, this isn't it — Italian Sausage Marinara is the tomato one, though it contains pork sausage and so doesn't work if you're avoiding meat. There is no meat-free tomato pasta on the standard menu, which is a genuine gap.

Price and Calories

Dish~$7.99~530–550
Bread bowl~$8.99Varies — check the app

On the calorie figure: Domino's own published guide has listed 530 and independent nutrition databases put it closer to 550. Call it about 540 and don't treat any single number as exact. Bread bowl entries vary more between sources than dish entries do, which is why there's no confident number in that row.

The Lightest Pasta — But Not Light

Against the rest of the pasta menu it wins clearly:

Pasta (dish)Calories

Chicken Alfredo~620
Italian Sausage Marinara~690
Chicken Carbonara~690

That's a real gap — roughly 150 calories below the heaviest options for the same money.

But it's worth being honest about what that means. "Vegetable" is not the same as "light." The cream sauce and cheese are doing most of the calorie work here, and at around 540 this is comparable to two slices of large cheese pizza. If you're specifically after the lightest thing on the menu, a garden salad or plain boneless chicken sits well below it — see our calories guide for the full comparison.

Vegetarian, Not Vegan

The distinction matters and it gets blurred constantly.

No meat, so vegetarians are fine. But the sauce and cheese are dairy, so it isn't vegan, and it isn't dairy-free for anyone avoiding milk. It also contains wheat and soy.

Domino's prepares everything in a shared kitchen with shared equipment, which is a separate issue from the ingredient list. If your restriction is a preference, that's usually acceptable. If it's a medical allergy, a menu description isn't a clearance and you should check Domino's current allergen information directly.

If you are vegan, the route that works is a build-your-own penne with Robust Inspired Tomato Sauce and vegetable toppings, ordered with no cheese. Our vegetarian and vegan guide covers exactly what qualifies across the whole menu.

The Leftovers Problem

One practical drawback that nobody mentions on a menu.

Cream sauces split when reheated. The fat separates from the liquid and the texture goes grainy — a microwave is particularly unkind to them. That makes Pasta Primavera a poor choice if you're ordering for one and expect to eat half tomorrow.

  • Best fix: an oven at low heat, covered, which holds the sauce together
  • Worst approach: a microwave on full power
  • Better plan: if leftovers are likely, the marinara pasta reheats without any of this trouble

Who It Suits

  • The vegetarian in a mixed group order — its main reason to exist, and a proper meal rather than an afterthought
  • Anyone who wants vegetables without a tomato sauce
  • Lunch for one, where a whole pizza is too much
  • Anyone choosing the lightest pasta — it is, by about 150 calories

And who it doesn't:

  • Vegans, and anyone avoiding dairy — the sauce rules it out
  • Anyone expecting a tomato pasta — read the name carefully
  • Anyone planning on leftovers — the sauce won't survive the reheat
  • Anyone avoiding gluten — it's wheat pasta, and there's no substitute version

  • Pair it with a salad rather than a bread side if you want to keep the meal from being carbohydrate on carbohydrate

title: Domino's Philly Cheese Steak Sandwich
description: Steak, onions, green peppers and mushrooms under provolone and American cheese, baked on artisan bread — the least pizza-like thing on the Domino's menu.
fullContent:
The Most Overlooked Thing on the Menu

Domino's sandwiches get almost no attention, which is a shame, because they're the reason Domino's works as a lunch stop rather than only a dinner one. They're baked on artisan bread in the same conveyor oven as the pizzas, so they arrive properly hot rather than sitting under a lamp.

The Philly Cheese Steak is the flagship: sliced steak with onions, green peppers and mushrooms under a blend of provolone and American cheese. No tomato sauce anywhere.

The Numbers

Philly Cheese SteakSmall pizza, for comparison
Example price~$7.99~$8.99
Calories~720~1,200
Protein~38gLower

That comparison is the useful one, and it's why this sandwich deserves more attention than it gets. For one person eating alone it's frequently the smarter buy than a small pizza — similar money, around 480 fewer calories, no leftovers going stale in a box, and it survives the trip better.

The protein figure is worth flagging separately. Roughly 38 grams is high for anything on this menu. If you're ordering with protein in mind rather than just calories, this is one of the strongest options Domino's sells.

The Sodium Problem

Now the part no menu is going to lead with, and the reason this page exists rather than just restating the description.

Published figures put a half sandwich at around 1,280mg of sodium. A whole one is therefore near 2,560mg — more than the 2,300mg daily limit US dietary guidelines suggest for an adult.

One sandwich is a full day's sodium. That's not a reason nobody should order it — plenty of fast food sits in this territory, and if you eat this occasionally it's unremarkable. But if you're managing blood pressure, or watching sodium on medical advice, this is the specific item on the Domino's menu to know about, and it's the kind of thing that gets buried three clicks into a nutrition PDF.

If that applies to you, the half sandwich is a genuinely useful option, and a plain boneless chicken order sits considerably lower on both sodium and calories.

How It Tastes

Savoury and cheese-heavy, with no tomato sauce anywhere. The two cheeses do different jobs — provolone for stretch, American for the melt — and the vegetables soften in the oven rather than staying crisp. The steak is sliced thin, so it reads as part of the filling rather than as a separate piece of meat.

If you like the Philly Cheese Steak pizza, this is the same flavour profile in a portable format. And if you've never tried either, this is the least pizza-like thing Domino's makes — which is exactly its appeal on a day when you don't want pizza but do want something from the same order.

Who It Suits

  • Solo lunch — the single best use case. No sharing, no leftovers
  • Anyone in a group who doesn't want pizza but is ordering with people who do
  • Protein-focused ordering — 38g is the strongest figure in this part of the menu
  • Carryout orders, where it arrives at its best

And who it doesn't:

  • Anyone watching sodium — a whole sandwich is a day's worth
  • Vegetarians — the Mediterranean Veggie is the meat-free sandwich
  • Anyone avoiding gluten or dairy — there's no gluten-free bread option for sandwiches, and the cheese is structural
  • Long deliveries — it's much better hot

Ordering It Well

  • Build it into a deal. Sandwiches are usually Mix & Match eligible, so adding one inside an offer costs less than buying it alongside a full-price pizza — our deal comparison covers which offer fits which basket
  • Eat it hot. Melted cheese is the whole structure of the thing; cold, it sets solid
  • Skip the extra dip. The sandwich already carries plenty of sodium and fat, and a ranch cup adds roughly 170 calories on top
  • Consider the half if you want the flavour without the full sodium load, or if it's accompanying something else

Where It Sits on the Menu

Against the other sandwiches, this is the savoury, vegetable-forward one — the Chicken Bacon Ranch is creamier and milder, and the Mediterranean Veggie is the meat-free option. Prices sit in the same band across all three, so the decision is flavour rather than value.

Against the wider menu, it's a rare thing at Domino's: a complete single-person meal that isn't a compromise. Most of the menu is built for sharing, and this isn't.

title: Domino's Chicken Bacon Ranch Sandwich
description: Grilled chicken, smoked bacon, creamy ranch and provolone baked on artisan bread — the richest sandwich Domino's makes, and the highest in protein.
fullContent:
The Rich One

Grilled chicken breast, smoked bacon, creamy ranch and provolone, baked on artisan bread in the same oven as the pizzas. This is the richest sandwich Domino's makes, and the one that most reliably divides people — because ranch is not a background note here, it's the whole dish.

The Numbers

Chicken Bacon RanchPhilly Cheese Steak
Calories~870~720
Protein~45g~38g
Sodium~2,160mg~2,560mg
Example price~$7.99~$7.99

That table contains the genuinely interesting thing about these two sandwiches, and it's not what you'd guess. The Chicken Bacon Ranch has ~150 more calories, but around 400mg less sodium.

So the two sandwiches are worse in different ways rather than one being simply heavier. If you're watching calories, the Philly is the better pick. If you're watching sodium — which is the one people rarely check — this one actually wins, despite being the richer sandwich.

The Protein Case

At roughly 45 grams, this is the highest-protein item in this part of the menu, and it's a genuinely strong figure for fast food. Grilled chicken breast and bacon both contribute, and unlike a lot of the menu, the protein isn't incidental.

If you order with macros in mind rather than calories alone, that changes the calculation. 870 calories carrying 45g of protein is a very different proposition from 870 calories of bread and cheese — for comparison, three slices of large pepperoni pizza land near 900 calories with substantially less protein.

The Sodium Note

Around 2,160mg for a whole sandwich, against the 2,300mg daily limit US dietary guidelines suggest for an adult. That's roughly 94% of a day in one item.

Worth knowing rather than worth panicking about — most fast food sits in this territory, and an occasional sandwich is unremarkable. But if you manage blood pressure or watch sodium on medical advice, the half sandwich is a genuinely useful option here, and it halves both figures at once.

Ranch Is the Whole Decision

Everything about whether you'll like this comes down to one question: do you like ranch?

It's creamy, tangy and mild, with no heat at all. The bacon supplies smoke and salt, the chicken keeps it from being purely rich, and the provolone melts into the sauce rather than sitting on top of it. If ranch isn't your thing, nothing else in the sandwich will rescue it — the Philly Cheese Steak is the savoury alternative.

If you already know you like the Cali Chicken Bacon Ranch pizza, this is the same combination in a portable format. Both are built on ranch instead of tomato sauce, which remains the most surprising thing on Domino's menu for anyone who has only ever ordered red-sauce pizzas.

Who It Suits

  • Anyone who likes ranch — this is the most ranch-forward item on the menu
  • Protein-focused ordering — 45g is the best figure in this category
  • Solo lunch or a late-night order — no sharing, no leftovers
  • Children — mild, familiar, no heat

And who it doesn't:

  • Anyone who dislikes ranch. There is no version of this without it
  • Anyone counting calories closely — it's the heaviest sandwich here
  • Anyone avoiding dairy or egg — the ranch rules out both
  • Anyone wanting heat — this is a mild sandwich

Ordering It Well

  • Don't add a ranch cup. The sandwich already has the sauce, and an extra cup puts roughly 170 calories on top of 870
  • Build it into a deal rather than adding it at the end — sandwiches are usually Mix & Match eligible, and our deal comparison covers which offer fits which order
  • Eat it hot. Ranch and melted provolone are excellent warm and unpleasant once they've set
  • Take the half if you want the flavour without the full calorie and sodium load

Where It Sits

Three sandwiches, three jobs. This is the creamy, indulgent one; the Philly Cheese Steak is savoury and vegetable-forward; the Mediterranean Veggie is the meat-free option. Prices sit in the same band, so it's a flavour decision, not a value one.

Against the wider menu, it's a complete single-person meal at a fair price with a serious protein figure attached — which is more than most of the Domino's menu can claim.

title: Domino's Mediterranean Veggie Sandwich
description: Spinach, feta, banana peppers, onions and tomatoes baked on artisan bread — Domino's only meat-free sandwich, and the lightest of the three.
fullContent:
The Only Meat-Free Sandwich

Domino's makes three oven-baked sandwiches and exactly one without meat in it. The Mediterranean Veggie is that one — baby spinach, feta, banana peppers, onions and diced tomatoes with provolone, baked on artisan bread in the same conveyor oven as the pizzas.

That single fact does most of the work here. If you're vegetarian and everyone else is ordering pizza, this is your hot, substantial alternative to picking at a bread side. There's no second option in this category, so the practical question isn't really which sandwich to choose — it's whether this one is any good.

The short answer is that it's better than it needs to be. On the numbers, it's the strongest sandwich on the menu.

How the Three Sandwiches Compare

This is the comparison nobody runs, and the results are not what most people would guess.

Mediterranean VeggiePhilly Cheese SteakChicken Bacon Ranch
Calories~680–700~720~870
Protein~32–36g~38g~45g
Sodium~2,050–2,220mg~2,560mg~2,160mg
Example price~$8.99~$7.99~$7.99

The vegetarian sandwich is the lowest of the three on calories and on sodium, and it's only a few grams behind on protein. That's an unusual outcome — the meat-free option on a fast-food menu is normally the consolation prize, not the best-balanced item in its category.

The one place it loses is price, and that's worth being blunt about.

The Awkward Bit: It Costs More

It commonly lists around $8.99 against roughly $7.99 for the two meat sandwiches. People notice this and find it irritating, reasonably so — the sandwich without steak or chicken in it is the expensive one.

Feta and the vegetable mix are the usual explanation, and feta genuinely is a more expensive cheese than mozzarella. Whether that justifies a dollar is your call. What it does mean practically is that if you don't eat meat, there's no cheaper sandwich to fall back on — this is the category, and it's priced where it's priced.

The mitigation is straightforward: sandwiches are usually eligible in Mix & Match style offers, so ordering it inside a deal rather than at menu price closes most of that gap. Our deal comparison covers which offer suits which basket.

Where the Protein Comes From

Around 32 to 36 grams is a genuinely strong figure for a sandwich with no meat in it, and it's worth understanding why, because it changes how you think about the item.

It's the cheese, not the vegetables. Feta and provolone are doing nearly all of that work. Spinach, onions and tomatoes contribute almost nothing to the protein count — they're there for flavour, texture and bulk.

That matters for two reasons. If you're vegetarian and ordering with protein in mind, this sandwich delivers, and it delivers more than most vegetarian fast food does. But if you're picturing a light salad-style item because it's the vegetable one, the cheese content is the thing to be realistic about. It's a cheese sandwich with vegetables in it more than the other way round.

Banana Peppers Are Not Spicy

The most common wrong expectation about this sandwich, and worth clearing up because it puts people off unnecessarily.

Banana peppers are tangy, not hot. They're mildly acidic and slightly sweet — closer to a pickle than a chilli. Nobody has ever found this sandwich too spicy, because there's no heat in it anywhere.

What they actually do is cut through the richness. Between feta and provolone, this sandwich has a lot of salt and fat in it, and the peppers and tomatoes are what stop it from being heavy. Remove them and it would be a much duller thing to eat.

How It Tastes

Brighter and sharper than the other two sandwiches. Feta is the defining flavour — salty and tangy in a way mozzarella isn't, and the reason a vegetable sandwich here doesn't taste flat.

The spinach wilts down in the oven rather than staying crisp, so don't expect salad texture. This is a baked, soft, savoury sandwich, and it's better for it. The onions sweeten as they cook, the tomatoes soften into the filling, and the whole thing holds together as one item rather than a pile of separate ingredients.

If you like the loaded pizzas but want something that isn't pizza, or you've had the Spinach & Feta pizza and enjoyed it, this is the flavour family you're already in.

Vegetarian, Not Vegan

Worth being precise about, because it's the question that actually matters to the people searching for this item.

No meat, so vegetarians are fine. Not vegan — both the feta and the provolone are dairy, and there is no vegan cheese on Domino's US menu, so there's no version of this sandwich that works. It also contains wheat and soy.

Domino's prepares everything in a shared kitchen with shared equipment, which is a separate consideration from the ingredient list. For a dietary preference that's generally fine; for a medical allergy it isn't, and a menu description is not an allergen clearance.

If you are vegan, the workable options are a cheeseless build-your-own pizza or a build-your-own pasta with Robust Inspired Tomato Sauce. Our vegetarian and vegan guide covers exactly what qualifies across the whole menu — and it's a shorter list than people expect.

Who It Suits

  • The vegetarian in a mixed group order — its main reason to exist, and a proper meal rather than an afterthought
  • Anyone who finds the ranch and steak sandwiches too heavy — this is the lighter one on the numbers as well as in feel
  • People who like feta and briny, tangy flavours
  • Solo lunch — no sharing, no leftovers, and it travels reasonably
  • Anyone watching sodium — it's the lowest of the three, though still substantial

And who it doesn't:

  • Vegans, and anyone avoiding dairy — the cheese is the whole sandwich
  • Anyone expecting heat from the banana peppers
  • Anyone avoiding gluten — there's no gluten-free bread for sandwiches
  • Anyone hoping for a light, salad-style item — it's cheese-forward

Ordering It Well

  • Put it inside a deal. This matters more here than on the other sandwiches, because it's the one with the price premium to offset
  • Eat it hot. Feta and provolone both set as they cool, and the sandwich is noticeably better fresh from the oven
  • Pair it with a salad rather than a bread side if you want to keep the meal from being bread on bread
  • Consider the half if it's accompanying something else, or if the sodium figure matters to you — it halves both numbers at once
  • Check availability. The sandwich lineup varies between franchises more than the pizza menu does

Where It Sits on the Menu

Against the other two sandwiches, this is the bright, sharp, lighter one — the Philly Cheese Steak is savoury and steak-led, the Chicken Bacon Ranch is creamy and the richest. The decision is flavour, with the caveat that this one costs a dollar more.

Against Domino's wider vegetarian range, it's one of a small number of genuinely substantial meat-free meals — alongside Pasta Primavera and the veggie specialty pizzas. That range is narrower than it should be for a menu this size, which is worth saying plainly rather than pretending the options are abundant.

title: Domino's Chocolate Lava Crunch Cakes
description: Two warm chocolate cakes with a molten centre — Domino's best-known dessert, and the one most sensitive to how long it sits in a bag.
fullContent:
The Dessert People Actually Order

Domino's dessert menu is short, and the Chocolate Lava Crunch Cakes are the reason most people look at it at all. Two warm chocolate cakes with a molten centre, baked so the middle stays liquid, served two to an order.

They're also the item on this menu most affected by something that has nothing to do with the recipe: how long they sit in a bag before you eat them. More on that below, because it's the difference between the dessert you ordered and an ordinary chocolate cake.

Price, Portion and Calories

Per cakePer order of two
Example price—~$4.99
Calories~350~700
Sugar~31g~62g
Fat~17g~34g
Sodium~150mg~300mg

Two figures in that table deserve pulling out, and they point in opposite directions.

The Sugar Number

This is the part worth knowing, and it isn't the calorie count.

A single lava cake carries around 31 grams of sugar. For context, the American Heart Association suggests a daily added-sugar limit of roughly 25 grams for women and 36 grams for men.

So one cake is approximately a full day's added sugar, and the order of two is close to double it. That's a more meaningful figure than the 700 calories, because calories from a dessert are at least expected — the sugar load catches people out, particularly anyone who ordered dessert thinking of it as a small extra rather than a substantial item.

None of which means don't order them. It means that if you're going to, sharing the order is the sensible default rather than a compromise — which happens to be exactly what the two-cake portion is designed for.

The One Number That's Low

Worth a fair word in the other direction: sodium is around 150mg per cake, which is genuinely low for anything on the Domino's menu.

By comparison, a single Philly Cheese Steak sandwich runs near 2,560mg. If you're watching sodium rather than sugar, dessert is not where your problem is on this menu.

Timing Is Everything

Here's the practical part, and the reason this page exists rather than just repeating the description.

The molten centre sets as the cake cools. That's simple physics, and no amount of packaging prevents it. A lava cake eaten straight after collection is a warm cake with liquid chocolate inside; the same cake twenty-five minutes into a delivery route is a perfectly nice chocolate cake with a soft middle — which is not what you paid for.

Two consequences that are genuinely useful:

  • Carryout is a meaningfully different product here. This is one of only two items on the menu where that's true — the other is Loaded Tots. Most food just arrives less hot; these arrive structurally changed
  • Eat them before the pizza, not after. Counterintuitive, but the cakes are far more time-sensitive than the pizza is. Pizza is fine slightly cool; a lava cake isn't

If they've already gone cold, a short spell in a warm oven does bring some of the centre back. A microwave is the wrong tool — it makes the cake rubbery while barely touching the middle.

How They Taste

Rich and straightforwardly sweet, with a firm outer cake and a genuinely liquid chocolate centre when fresh. The texture contrast is the whole appeal — without it you're eating a decent but unremarkable chocolate pudding.

They're small, which is easy to underestimate. At roughly 85 grams each these are not large cakes, and 350 calories in something that size tells you how dense they are. That's not a criticism — it's why one is genuinely enough for most people.

Which Dessert to Order

Domino's has three desserts, and the honest advice is to choose by how many people you're feeding rather than by flavour. All three are sweet and priced within a couple of dollars of each other.

DessertPiecesExample priceFeeds
Lava Crunch Cakes2~$4.992 people
Cinnamon Bread Twists8~$5.993–4 people
Marbled Cookie Brownie9~$6.994–5 people

Lava cakes are the cheapest dessert and the one that splits most cleanly between two. Two cakes, two people, no negotiation. For a group of four they're the wrong choice — somebody misses out, and buying two orders is more expensive than one tray of something else.

Who It Suits

  • Two people sharing — the portion is designed for exactly this
  • Carryout orders, where they arrive as intended
  • Anyone wanting dessert without buying a whole tray
  • Anyone watching sodium rather than sugar

And who it doesn't:

  • Groups of four or more — the twists or the brownie divide properly
  • Long deliveries — the centre sets before it reaches you
  • Anyone limiting sugar — one cake is roughly a day's worth
  • Vegans — dairy and egg, and there's no vegan dessert on the US menu

Ordering Them Well

  • Add them inside a deal, not after it. Desserts are usually Mix & Match eligible, and adding one at the end at menu price is the most expensive route — see our deal comparison
  • Take carryout if the dessert matters to the meal rather than being an afterthought
  • Don't over-order. One pair between two is plenty; two pairs between two is a great deal of chocolate
  • Check allergens — wheat, dairy, egg and soy are all present

title: Domino's Cinnamon Bread Twists
description: Eight freshly baked bread twists dusted with cinnamon and sugar, served with sweet icing — the Domino's dessert built for sharing.
fullContent:
The Sharing Dessert

Cinnamon Bread Twists are the same twisted bread as Domino's savoury sides, baked golden and then dusted with cinnamon and sugar, served with a cup of sweet icing for dipping. Eight pieces to an order, and that piece count is the whole reason to choose them.

Domino's has three desserts and they're priced within two dollars of each other, so the useful way to pick isn't flavour — it's how many people you're feeding.

Choosing by Portion, Not Flavour

DessertPiecesExample priceFeeds
Lava Crunch Cakes2~$4.992 people
Cinnamon Bread Twists8~$5.993–4 people
Marbled Cookie Brownie9~$6.994–5 people

Two lava cakes around a table of four means somebody misses out. Eight twists divides cleanly and nobody has to be polite about it. That's not a small consideration when dessert arrives at the end of a shared meal.

The Calorie Figure, Honestly

This page is going to be less confident than most, because the published data genuinely doesn't agree with itself.

The commonly cited serving figure is around 250 calories for two pieces. But the totals different databases give for a full eight-piece order aren't consistent with that — some imply a little over 500 for the whole order, others imply closer to 1,000. Those can't both be right, and the gap is too wide to average away.

So rather than pick a number and present it as fact: treat 250 per two pieces as the reliable figure, and read the live total in the Domino's app if the full-order number matters to you. This is exactly the kind of item where the app's own calculator is worth thirty seconds of your time.

What is clear either way is the direction of travel. This is fried-adjacent sweet bread with sugar on the outside and icing on the side — it's a dessert, it eats like one, and it's easy to eat several pieces without noticing, in the way shared bread always is.

How They Taste

Soft rather than crisp, with cinnamon sugar on the outside and fairly plain bread inside. The twist itself is much less sweet than the coating suggests, which is why the icing cup matters more than it looks like it should.

  • Dipped: properly sweet, and closer to a cinnamon roll
  • Undipped: mildly sweet bread — pleasant, but underwhelming as a dessert

If you find most desserts too sweet, that's actually useful: you control the sweetness by how much icing you use, which isn't true of the lava cakes or the brownie.

They Travel Well — And That Matters

Their quiet advantage over the lava cakes.

There's no molten centre to set, so a long delivery costs you some warmth and nothing else. Lava cakes are structurally different after twenty-five minutes in a bag; these are just cooler.

Which gives a simple rule for ordering dessert at Domino's:

  • Short delivery or carryout: lava cakes, at their best
  • Long delivery: these, or the Cookie Brownie

They also reheat well — a few minutes in a warm oven brings them close to fresh, which is not something you can do successfully with a set lava cake.

Who It Suits

  • Groups of three or four — the portion divides properly
  • Long deliveries, where the time-sensitive desserts fall down
  • Anyone who prefers bread-based desserts to cake
  • People who find desserts too sweet — you control the icing
  • Children, since the pieces are small and easy to handle

And who it doesn't:

  • One or two people — eight pieces is too many, and lava cakes are cheaper
  • Vegans — they contain milk, like every Domino's bread side
  • Anyone avoiding gluten — there's no alternative version
  • Anyone wanting a rich, chocolatey dessert — this is bread, not cake

Ordering Them Well

  • Build them into a deal. Desserts are usually Mix & Match eligible, so adding one inside an offer costs less than adding it at menu price at the end — our deal comparison covers which offer fits which basket
  • Ask for the icing on the side if you'd rather control the sweetness. It usually comes that way
  • Treat them as replacing a bread side, not adding to one. If you've already ordered garlic twists or cheesy bread, this is a lot of the same bread twice
  • Eat them warm. They firm up noticeably as they cool

Where They Sit

Against the other two desserts, these are the middle option in every sense — more pieces than the lava cakes, fewer than the brownie, and the least rich of the three. That makes them the safe choice when you don't know the table's preferences, and the right choice when the delivery is long.

Against the wider menu, they're one of the few Domino's items where the honest advice is to order them instead of something rather than as well as it. A bread dessert after a bread side after a pizza is a lot of the same thing in one meal.

title: Domino's Marbled Cookie Brownie
description: Cookie dough and brownie batter marbled together, baked as a tray and cut into nine pieces — the Domino's dessert that feeds a group.
fullContent:
The Group Dessert

The Marbled Cookie Brownie is exactly what the name describes: cookie dough and brownie batter swirled together, baked as a single tray and cut into nine pieces. It's the largest dessert portion Domino's sells, and the only one that genuinely stretches across a table.

Domino's has three desserts priced within two dollars of each other, so the useful way to choose isn't flavour — it's how many people you're feeding. This is the one for a crowd.

The Numbers

Per pieceWhole tray (9)
Calories~190~1,710
Sugar~18g~162g
Fat~9g~81g
Example price—~$6.99

Per piece, this is the lightest dessert Domino's makes — 190 calories against roughly 350 for a lava cake. That's genuinely useful if you want something sweet without committing to much.

The tray total is the number that deserves respect. Around 1,710 calories and 162 grams of sugar sitting in an open box on a coffee table is a different proposition from a portion you were served. Split five ways it's about two pieces and 380 calories each, which is reasonable. Left open during a film with three people, it isn't.

That's not an argument against it. It's an argument for cutting it up and handing it round rather than leaving the box open, which is how most of it gets eaten without anyone deciding to.

Value: The Honest Comparison

DessertPiecesExample priceFeedsCost per person
Lava Crunch Cakes2~$4.992~$2.50
Cinnamon Bread Twists8~$5.993–4~$1.70
Marbled Cookie Brownie9~$6.994–5~$1.55

It's the most expensive dessert per order and the cheapest per person. Those aren't contradictory — they're the whole reason the portion exists.

For two people it's the wrong choice. You'll pay two dollars more than the lava cakes and be eating brownie for two days. For five, nothing else on the menu covers the table without buying multiple orders.

How It Tastes

Because the batters are marbled rather than layered, each piece carries both textures — the chew of a cookie and the denser, fudgier brownie running through it. You don't get a cookie piece and a brownie piece; you get both in every square.

It's sweeter and denser than the bread twists and less dramatic than a lava cake. There's no molten centre, no textural surprise — just a solid, good baked dessert. That sounds like faint praise but it's actually the point: it's the most reliable dessert on the menu precisely because nothing about it can go wrong in transit.

The Delivery Advantage

This is where it quietly beats everything else on the dessert menu.

Nothing about it depends on arriving hot. Lava cakes have a molten centre that sets on a long drive — a genuinely different product after twenty-five minutes in a bag. Bread twists lose warmth. The brownie tray just... arrives, and it's exactly the same as it was.

So the dessert rule at Domino's is straightforward:

  • Carryout or short delivery: lava cakes, at their best
  • Long delivery: this, or the twists
  • Feeding four or more: this, regardless of distance

Leftovers Actually Work

Worth flagging because it's rare on this menu. Baked cookie and brownie keep perfectly well overnight in a sealed container — no reheating needed, no texture collapse, nothing that suffers.

Compare that with the rest of a Domino's order: pizza is acceptable cold but not good, pasta with cream sauce splits when reheated, tots are ruined within half an hour. The brownie is the one item where buying more than you'll eat tonight is a reasonable plan rather than a mistake.

Which slightly changes the "too much for two people" advice above. If you don't mind brownie tomorrow, the tray is fine for two — you're just buying two desserts.

Who It Suits

  • Four or five people — the only Domino's dessert that stretches that far
  • Long deliveries, since nothing about it is time-sensitive
  • Parties, film nights, office orders — a tray beats individual portions
  • Anyone who wants a small sweet thing — one piece at 190 calories is the lightest dessert option here
  • People who don't mind leftovers

And who it doesn't:

  • One or two people who won't keep leftovers — lava cakes are cheaper and better portioned
  • Vegans — dairy and egg
  • Anyone avoiding gluten — there's no alternative version
  • Anyone wanting the molten-centre experience — that's the lava cakes

Ordering It Well

  • Add it inside a deal. Desserts are usually Mix & Match eligible, and adding one at the end at menu price is the most expensive route — our deal comparison covers which offer fits which basket
  • Portion it before you sit down. An open tray is how 1,710 calories disappears without anyone deciding to eat it
  • Order it for the group size, not the flavour. Four or more people, this one; two people, the lava cakes
  • Check allergens — wheat, dairy, egg and soy are all present

Where It Sits

Against the other two desserts, this is the biggest, the most reliable and the cheapest per head. It's also the least exciting, and that's a fair trade — you're buying dependability and coverage rather than a moment.

Against the wider menu, it's the only Domino's item where leftovers are genuinely as good the next day. That's worth something on a menu built almost entirely around food that's best in the first fifteen minutes.

title: Domino's Parmesan Bread Bites
description: Sixteen small baked bread bites brushed with garlic and Parmesan — the cheapest side on the Domino's menu and the easiest to share.
fullContent:
The Best Value Side on the Menu

Sixteen small baked bread bites, brushed with garlic seasoning and Parmesan, for around $4.99. Per piece, nothing else on the Domino's menu comes close on value — and the portion is the easiest to pass around a table without anyone measuring their share.

That second point matters more than it sounds, and it's the main reason to choose these over the twists.

Price Against the Other Bread Sides

SidePiecesExample priceCost per piece
Parmesan Bread Bites16~$4.99~31¢
Garlic Bread Twists8~$5.99~75¢
Stuffed Cheesy Bread8~$7.99~$1.00

The bites are the cheapest order and carry twice the piece count. The pieces are smaller, so it isn't twice the bread — but on cost per mouthful and on how well the portion divides, they win comfortably.

The Calorie Figure, Honestly

This page has to be less confident than most, because the published data contradicts itself.

One source puts a full 16-piece order at around 590 calories, with a stated weight of 220g — a figure that's internally plausible for that much bread. Elsewhere, per-serving listings for four pieces imply a considerably higher total for the order. Those two cannot both be right, and the gap is too wide to split the difference.

So: treat around 590 for the whole order as the working figure, and if you need precision, read the live number in the Domino's app. This is the kind of item where thirty seconds with the official calculator beats any chart, including this one.

What's not in dispute is the direction. This is bread brushed with butter-flavoured spread and cheese — it's a side, it eats like one, and it's easy to keep reaching for because the pieces are small.

Sodium and Protein

Two figures worth having:

  • Sodium: around 770mg for the full order. Moderate by this menu's standards — a fraction of what a Philly Cheese Steak sandwich carries, but not nothing if you're already having something salty
  • Protein: around 20g across the order, which is more than you'd expect from bread. The cheese is responsible

How They Taste

Small, soft and garlicky, with Parmesan on the outside rather than inside. They're closer to seasoned dinner rolls than to breadsticks — there's no crisp shell and no cheese pull, because there's no cheese filling.

They're fairly plain on their own, which is deliberate. The dipping cup does real work here, and that makes them more flexible than a heavily seasoned side: a table can take them in different directions depending on what they dip into.

Why the Piece Count Wins

The genuinely practical argument for these over the twists, and it's about arithmetic rather than flavour.

  • Sixteen bites among four people: four each, no negotiation
  • Eight twists among four people: two each, and immediately awkward if someone wants a third

Small pieces also mean people take what they want rather than committing to a large portion, which is why a bites order tends to get finished while a twists order often leaves two pieces going cold. If you're ordering for a group and you don't know their appetites, the bites are the lower-risk choice.

The Dip Decision

Because the bites are mild, what you dip them in changes the whole side — and it changes the calorie count more than people realise:

  • Marinara — around 45 calories a cup. The light choice, and usually included
  • Ranch or blue cheese — roughly 100 to 170 a cup
  • Garlic and butter style dips — the heaviest of the lot

Two or three creamy cups across a shared bread side can add as much as several extra bites would. Not a reason to skip them — a reason to know. Full numbers are in our calories guide.

Who It Suits

  • Sharing around three or four people — the portion divides better than anything else here
  • Ordering on a budget — the cheapest way to add something to a pizza order
  • Children, since the pieces are small and mild
  • Mixed tables, where the dip lets people take it in different directions

And who it doesn't:

  • Anyone wanting the cheese-pull experience — that's Stuffed Cheesy Bread
  • Vegans — all Domino's bread sides contain milk
  • Anyone avoiding gluten
  • One person wanting a substantial side — sixteen small bites is a sharing portion

Ordering Them Well

  • Build them into a deal. They're usually Mix & Match eligible, which makes an already cheap side cheaper — see our deal comparison
  • One shared side per three or four people is the rule that stops food going home in a box
  • Eat them early. Small pieces cool fast — faster than twists, and much faster than a pizza
  • Take the marinara if you want a dip without thinking about the calorie cost

Where They Sit

Against the other bread sides, these are the cheapest, the most shareable and the mildest. The garlic twists are more substantial per piece and better for dipping; Stuffed Cheesy Bread is the indulgent one and roughly three dollars more.

Against the wider menu, they're the item to reach for when you want to add something to an order without adding much to the bill — which, on a menu where sides routinely cost as much as a pizza, is a genuinely useful thing to have.
